newsitem.title: USA: Tragic testimony as U.S. seeks death for McVeigh.
newsitem.headline: Tragic testimony as U.S. seeks death for McVeigh.

text.p: Tearful relatives of Oklahoma City bombing victims told of terrible injuries, broken hearts, mental trauma and ruined lives as prosecutors called on Wednesday for convicted bomber Timothy McVeigh to be sentenced to death.

"I feel like my heart looks like that building and has a huge hole that never can be mended," said a weeping Diane Leonard, whose husband, Secret Service agent Donald Leonard, was killed in the April 19, 1995, truck bombing that destroyed the Oklahoma City federal building.

"I feel like I died too on April 19," she said on the first day of the phase of the trial, in which the jury of seven men and five women will decide whether McVeigh should be executed by injection or spend the rest of his life in prison.

"Blake was my life. For months after the bombing I didn't care what happened to me. I didn't care if I lived or died," said auditor Laura Kennedy, 28, referring to her 18-month-old son who was killed in the day care centre of the federal building.
They were among 15 survivors, victims' relatives and rescue workers called by prosecutors to try to convince the jury that death was the only suitable punishment for McVeigh.
McVeigh was found guilty on Monday of blowing up the Alfred P. Murrah building, killing 168 people in the worst attack on civilians on U.S. soil.
"We will ask you to return a verdict of death, the only verdict that justly fits this crime," a solemn prosecutor Pat Ryan said during his opening statement in the penalty phase.
He said McVeigh, a 29-year-old Gulf War veteran, deserved to die because of seven aggravating factors, including his careful planning of the attack and the large number of victims.
In a heart-rending day, several witnesses broke down and cried as they relived the shock of losing loved ones. Relatives of bombing victims in court, journalists and several jurors wiped away tears.
McVeigh, who prosecutors say is a right-wing fanatic driven by hatred of the government, showed no emotion. Grim-looking defence lawyers did not cross-examine the witnesses.
Federal Judge Richard Matsch told jurors at the end of the day that their decision should be based on reason, not emotion.
"They (witnesses) cried and you cried. However, we are not here to seek revenge on Timothy McVeigh," he said. "Try to suppress some of the emotional reaction that it is natural to have."

Chief prosecutor Joe Hartzler said the prosecution expects to end its case sometime on Thursday afternoon and Matsch told defence attorney Stephen Jones to be ready to give his opening statement on Friday. Defence lawyers will call witnesses to try to show why McVeigh's life should be spared. Legal analysts say they face a daunting task.
Kathleen Treanor told how her mother- and father-in-law and her 4-year-old daughter Ashley Eckles were killed in the Social Security Administration office in the Murrah building.

Months later the medical examiner's office called her and said they had found part of her daughter's hand and asked whether she wanted it. "I said of course I want it. It's a part of her," Treanor said. Seven jurors were in tears at this point.
Susan Walton, 46, who was going into the Federal Employees Credit Union in the building when the bomb went off, suffered severe leg injuries and testified from a wheelchair.

Prosecutors showed jurors a video of Brandon Denny, 5, who was struck on the head by a ceiling tile, doing physical therapy. The boy, in a blue sweatsuit, had great difficulty lifting objects with his stiff right arm.
David Klaus, whose 29-year-old daughter Kimberly died in the blast, said he had suffered from depression, bronchitis, hepatitis and pneumonia and had lost weight since the bombing.
"It's been physically and emotionally just devastating for me," he said.

Mathilda Westberry said her grandson, David, had had severe emotional problems since the death of her husband Robert in the bombing. At school David sat with his hands over his ears, afraid his school would be blown up, she testified.

Alan Prokop, an Oklahoma City police officer and one of the first rescuers on scene, said a woman's hand protruding from the rubble clutched his hand. "Then her hand got very still and started to get cold. I felt her wrist for a pulse and I found none," he said.

Jerry Flowers, an Oklahoma City police sergeant, said one woman, trapped with water rising to her neck, screamed: "Don't let me drown." The water stopped rising just after it reached her chin, Flowers said, without saying what happened to her in the end. Later, he said, he pulled dead babies from the second-floor day care centre.
